before.label: Economic history
before.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.

before.label: Ivy Pinchbeck
before.description: Makes women’s labour central to the history of industrialization, including agricultural, domestic, and factory work. Distinguishes changes in workplace and payment from the mistaken assumption that women only began productive work with factories. Her account belongs to interwar economic and women’s history, before the later expansion of feminist scholarship.

after.label: Ivy Pinchbeck
after.description: Reconstructs women’s work before and during industrialization through household production, wages, training and agricultural change. She emphasizes unequal disruption while arguing for eventual benefits, a position distinct from Clark’s account of capitalist development.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930; new preface in the 1969 reprint). The original preface acknowledges Eileen Power’s direction of the research and Lilian Knowles’s earlier guidance.
after.scope_note: The complete 1930 introduction distinguishes paid visibility from productive work itself and separates married women, single women and workers supporting families. Power directs the acknowledged research; Knowles gives early guidance and Dorothy George supplies specific evidence. The 1969 preface, signed 1968, calls for later occupational research without supplying it. The broad optimistic conclusion remains an attributed argument; most occupational chapters and the original conclusion are unread.

before.label: Alice Clark
before.description: Investigates women’s working lives through household, occupational, and institutional records. Relates changes in women’s economic position to transformations in production and capitalism. Her broad account of change is an argument to test, not evidence that all women shared one experience or that later historians accepted her conclusions.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919). Compare with Pinchbeck’s later-period study to examine how historians explain the relationship between economic change and women’s autonomy.

after.label: Alice Clark
after.description: Studies women’s paid and unpaid production through overlapping household and capitalist arrangements. Differences of class and marital position shape her account of changing work, training and authority; her chronology and assumptions about earlier households remain contested.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919). Compare with Pinchbeck’s later-period study to examine how historians explain the relationship between economic change and women’s autonomy.
after.scope_note: The 1919 preface credits Schreiner, Knowles and Power’s unpublished research. Introduction and conclusion distinguish production for use, family enterprise and individual wages, while admitting conjectural medieval comparisons and incomplete causal evidence. Maternal and racial assumptions belong to Clark’s historical position. Erickson’s 1992 introduction values unpaid-work analysis while disputing chronology and household equality. Main occupational cases are not newly read; neither timeless equality nor a uniform decline for all women is established.

before.label: Eileen Power
before.description: Connects economic institutions and social life with the study of medieval women and ordinary people. Scholarship, teaching, broadcasting, and collaboration broaden her audiences. Her work contributes to both women’s history and economic history, and her direction of Pinchbeck’s research supplies a documented connection between generations of women historians.
